# Wisdom of Solomon Chapter 12 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Disagreement 1 — WIS 12:1: "incorruptible" vs. "imperishable" — the Spirit's attribute

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "your incorruptible Spirit is in all things" |
| LOGOS | "your imperishable Spirit is in all things" |
| PNEUMA | "Your imperishable Spirit permeates all things" |

**Issue:** Greek aphtharton — "imperishable, incorruptible, undying." Both "incorruptible" and "imperishable" are valid. "Incorruptible" carries a moral connotation (incapable of being corrupted/bribed); "imperishable" is more ontological (not subject to decay). In context, the ontological sense is primary — the Spirit is not subject to the deterioration that affects created things.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "your imperishable Spirit is in all things" (LOGOS). The verse establishes God's omnipresence through his Spirit, grounding the subsequent argument about universal divine care. "Imperishable" is the better ontological term here.

---

## Disagreement 2 — WIS 12:5: Canaanite rites — "initiatory rites" vs. "initiation" vs. "their initiation rites"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "sacrificial feasts of human flesh and blood, from the midst of an initiation" |
| LOGOS | "sacrificial feasts of human flesh and blood conducted in the midst of initiatory rites" |
| PNEUMA | "sacrificial feasts involving human flesh and blood conducted at the center of their initiation rites" |

**Issue:** Greek ek mesou thiasotas — "from the midst of a thiasōtēs" — a thiasōs was a cult group or religious fraternity involved in mystery rites. EMET's "an initiation" is too sparse; LOGOS and PNEUMA both capture the sense adequately. The Canaanite practices described (child sacrifice, cannibalistic feasts) are polemically depicted; historical accuracy is secondary to the rhetorical argument.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "sacrificial feasts of human flesh and blood conducted in the midst of initiatory rites" (LOGOS). The addition of "conducted in the midst of" makes the phrase grammatically cleaner than "from the midst of."

---

## Disagreement 3 — WIS 12:10: "way-of-thinking would not change" — the Canaanites' moral incapacity

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "their way-of-thinking would not change for an age" |
| LOGOS | "their way of thinking would never change" |
| PNEUMA | "their mindset would never truly change" |

**Issue:** Greek hoti ponēra hē genesis autōn kai emphytos hē kakia — "their origin was evil and their wickedness was inborn/natural." The theological claim here is that some peoples are so deeply corrupted that repentance is structurally impossible for them; yet God still gives them time. LOGOS and PNEUMA both render this adequately; EMET's "for an age" adds a temporal qualifier not strongly in the Greek.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "their way of thinking would never change" (LOGOS). Clear and direct. PNEUMA's "mindset" is acceptable but slightly anachronistic as a psychological term.

---

## Disagreement 4 — WIS 12:16: "strength is the beginning of righteousness" vs. "source"

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "your strength is the beginning of righteousness" |
| LOGOS | "your strength is the source of righteousness" |
| PNEUMA | "Your strength is precisely what makes you just" |

**Issue:** Greek archē — "beginning, origin, first principle." In Greek philosophy, archē is the foundational first principle of all things. The verse makes a philosophical claim: God's omnipotence is the ontological ground of his justice (he does not need to be unjust to survive). EMET's "beginning" is literal; LOGOS's "source" is philosophical; PNEUMA paraphrases into a consequence rather than a principle.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "your strength is the source of righteousness" (LOGOS). "Source" preserves the philosophical sense of archē as first principle without requiring the reader to unpack "beginning" philosophically.

---

## Disagreement 5 — WIS 12:22: "scourge our enemies a thousand-fold" — the Greek myriakis

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "you scourge our enemies a thousand-fold" |
| LOGOS | "you scourge our enemies ten-thousandfold" |
| PNEUMA | "you strike our enemies with blows a thousand times greater" |

**Issue:** Greek myriakis — "ten thousand times, innumerable times." Myrios = 10,000 in classical Greek (hence "myriad"). EMET's "a thousand-fold" mistranslates this as chiliakis. LOGOS correctly renders myriakis as "ten-thousandfold." PNEUMA's "a thousand times greater" also mistranslates.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "you scourge our enemies ten-thousandfold" (LOGOS). This is a straightforward translation accuracy issue: myriakis = ten thousand times, not one thousand.

---

## Disagreement 6 — WIS 12:25-26: "mockery-judgments" and "playful rebuke" — the tone of minor punishments

| Translator | Rendering |
|---|---|
| EMET | "as to unreasoning children you sent a judgment in mockery... those who were-not corrected by mockery-judgments" |
| LOGOS | "as to unreasoning children, you sent a judgment that mocked them... those who would not be corrected by a playful rebuke" |
| PNEUMA | "you sent them a judgment that matched their foolishness... those who laughed off the gentle, mocking correction" |

**Issue:** Greek empaigmoni katakrinei — "judgment in mockery/derision." The author argues that the minor plagues were themselves a form of divine satire — the punishment fitted the absurdity of the crime (worshipping insects). LOGOS's "playful rebuke" is the best rendering of the lesser punishment; PNEUMA's "laughed off" adds ironic wordplay but imports emotional content not in the Greek.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** LOGOS for both verses. "A judgment that mocked them" (v.25) and "a playful rebuke" (v.26) maintain the rhetorical register without over-dramatizing.
